solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Express extreme anger with a female, Italian, after short fling

indicators.note: a 'short' fling is THROW cut off before its last letter

blocks.note: fling = THROW, docked of its W
W is the standard abbreviation for with
IT = Italian, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: Someone flies into a rage over a brief romance with an Italian woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the shortened fling at the front, so the clue's second half is read first; the answer splits THRO-W-A-F-IT across what look like the words THROW A FIT.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the fit is a sudden outburst, so throwing one is a dramatic show of rage.

clue.text: Best chapter about current subject

indicators.note: 'about' turns C and I round so chapter comes last

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A reader picks out the best chapter on a topical issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current subject' looks like one phrase meaning a topical issue; 'current' is really I, the physicist's symbol, and 'subject' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the subject of a talk or essay is its topic.

clue.text: Theatrical company to mount repeat performance

blocks.note: a rep is a repertory theatre company

explanation.surface: A theatre troupe plans to stage a show a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' is the theatre word for staging a show, which fits the surface perfectly; here it just means go up, RISE.
explanation.definitionFit: From French reprendre, to take up again: a song or scene played again later in a show.

clue.text: Background? Western tabloid includes everything!

indicators.note: the Western tabloid 'includes' everything by holding it inside

blocks.note: a tabloid is a kind of newspaper

explanation.surface: A cowboy newspaper boasts that it covers every story going.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads like a tabloid's boast about its coverage. The question mark flags that wallpaper is only one kind of background.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: wallpaper forms the backdrop of a room, and a screen's background image is also called wallpaper.

clue.text: Outcry involving the Royal Marines, in addition

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so the outcry wraps round THE RM

blocks.note: furore = an outcry (British spelling, with the final E)

explanation.surface: A public row breaks out over the Royal Marines, as an added complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling FURORE, usual in Britain, matters: FUROR would leave the answer one E short.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both introduce an extra point in an argument.

clue.text: Boy, extremely drunk, was removed

indicators.note: 'was removed' tells you to take the letters WAS away

explanation.surface: A lad who got very drunk was thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was removed' reads as the passive of throwing someone out; it is an instruction to remove the letters WAS. 'Extremely' tempts you to take the outer letters of DRUNK, which gives nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword convention lets 'boy' stand for any boy's name; Ted is short for Edward.

clue.text: Refill tankard about finished

indicators.note: 'about' turns the tankard round

blocks.note: a pot is a drinking vessel, like a tankard

explanation.surface: A barman fills a tankard again once the drinker has emptied it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tankard' is POT, the old word for a drinking mug, and 'finished' is UP, as in 'time's up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: topping up a glass fills it back to the brim.

clue.text: Rendezvous with lover in Coventry Street

indicators.note: the answer sits in the letters of 'Coventry Street'

blocks.note: the end of Coventry plus the start of Street

explanation.surface: Two lovers arrange to meet on Coventry Street, near London's Leicester Square.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition takes up most of the clue, leaving just the street name as the hiding place: coven-TRY ST-reet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is specifically a meeting between lovers, so the definition spells out both halves of it.

clue.text: Play on words impressing educated girl, a moralist

indicators.note: to impress is to press into, so RITA goes into PUN

blocks.note: a pun is a play on words
from the play and film Educating Rita

explanation.surface: A witty remark wins over a well-read girl who turns out to be a prig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Educated girl' points to Rita of Willy Russell's Educating Rita, about a working-class woman's education.
explanation.definitionFit: The Puritans were strict Protestant reformers, and the word now means anyone rigid about morals.

clue.text: Fanciful hope conveyed about a male

blocks.note: piped = conveyed, as water through a pipe

explanation.surface: Someone voices a romantic wish about a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container or reversal signal; here it is simply RE.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from the visions of opium smokers, so it names a hope with no footing in reality.

clue.text: Well-liked university in London area

indicators.note: the university sits 'in' the London district

blocks.note: Poplar is a district of East London

explanation.surface: A London university is described as well regarded.
explanation.walkthrough: Poplar is a district in the East End of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something popular is liked by many people.

clue.text: Outing may produce pay dirt

indicators.note: the letters of PAY DIRT can produce something else

explanation.surface: A prospecting trip might strike gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Pay dirt is ground rich enough in gold to be worth mining, which gives the surface its prospecting sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an outing is a short pleasure trip, usually there and back in a day.

clue.text: Firm in time of difficulty is lacking power

indicators.note: the crisis is 'lacking' the letters IS

blocks.note: a crisis is a time of difficulty
the letters to take out, leaving CRIS

explanation.surface: A business struggling through a crisis has lost its energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' is a company in the surface and an adjective in the answer; 'is lacking' reads as grammar but 'is' is the letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of texture: crisp lettuce or a crisp biscuit is firm and brittle.

clue.text: The man told about one held back

indicators.note: 'told' goes round, 'about', the one

explanation.surface: A man speaks of someone who was kept in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held back' looks like part of the story about the one person; it is the definition, a past-tense verb matching HESITATED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who hesitated held back from acting for a moment.

clue.text: Style of writing supported by newspaper chief needing more staff

indicators.note: in a down clue what supports something sits beneath it, so ED comes after

blocks.note: shorthand is a style of rapid writing
ED = editor, chief of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A writing style is backed by an editor who complains of too few reporters.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper setting makes 'style of writing' look like house style; it is the reporter's shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands are workers, so being short of hands means not having enough staff.

clue.text: What sounds like bent grass?

indicators.note: the clue asks outright for a word that sounds like 'bent'

blocks.note: wry = bent, twisted, as in a wry neck

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what a curved blade of grass sounds like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent grass' is a real phrase, since bent is itself a grass; here 'bent' means twisted, WRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: rye is one of the cereal grasses, grown for grain and whisky.

clue.text: Presses so fervently to regain ownership

indicators.note: fervent action throws the letters about

explanation.surface: A creditor pushes hard to take back their goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presses' reads as the verb of the surface, but it is anagram fodder along with 'so'.
explanation.definitionFit: RE- plus POSSESS: to possess again, typically goods seized when payments stop.

clue.text: Particular action of knight, say, brought in of necessity

indicators.note: the knight is 'brought in' to the phrase for necessity

blocks.note: a knight is one example of a chess man

explanation.surface: A knight's deed was one he had no choice about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knight, say' tempts you towards SIR or N; the 'say' signals an example, here a chess piece, a MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The sense is the doing of a task, as in the performance of a duty, not a show on stage.

clue.text: Duck from Grasmere cooked around noon

indicators.note: cooking a thing changes its form, so the letters of Grasmere get mixed
the mixed letters go 'around' the N

explanation.surface: A duck from the Lake District village of Grasmere is roasted for lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like a verb, dodging out of Grasmere; it is the bird. Grasmere is a lake and village in England's Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the merganser is a fish-eating diving duck with a saw-edged bill.

clue.text: A seabird shown in advertisement in lift

indicators.note: the bird is 'shown in' the advertisement, printed inside it

explanation.surface: A seabird appears on a poster displayed in an elevator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' is the British word for an elevator; a paternoster is an old doorless kind whose cars circulate continuously.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the lift is named after the rosary, whose beads loop round like its chain of cars.

clue.text: Passage from North and South in characteristic setting

indicators.note: N and S go 'in' the characteristic
the characteristic is their 'setting', the thing they are set in

explanation.surface: A passage from Gaskell's novel North and South, in its typical setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage from North and South' reads as an extract from Gaskell's novel; 'from' is only a link to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the travel sense: goods in transit are in passage between places.

clue.text: The total, presumably? Only part

indicators.note: only part of 'presumably' is wanted

blocks.note: letters four to six of the word

explanation.surface: Someone guesses at a total, then admits they have only part of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'presumably' holds the answer in its middle: pre-SUM-ably.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the sum of some numbers is their total.

clue.text: Concubine some woman at Lusaka upset

indicators.note: only some of the letters of 'woman at Lusaka' are used
in a down clue, upset turns the letters upside down, reading them bottom to top

explanation.surface: A woman in Lusaka, the capital of Zambia, is distressed at being a concubine.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs backwards across three words, from the S of Lusaka up to the A of woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The feminine of sultan: besides a sultan's wife or mother, it once meant a king's mistress.

clue.text: Thus, a popular time for Coronation Street, for example

blocks.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Coronation Street wins a popular prime-time slot.
explanation.walkthrough: Coronation Street is a long-running British TV soap set in a northern English street.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'for example': Coronation Street has run on British TV since 1960.

clue.text: Working on island on tear-jerker?

blocks.note: on = working, as a machine is on

explanation.surface: Someone is busy on an island writing a sentimental weepie.
explanation.walkthrough: A tear-jerker is normally a sad film; the question mark allows the literal sense, something that makes you cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting an onion releases a gas that makes your eyes water.

clue.text: Off the cuff remark from a Liberal Democrat inside

indicators.note: Democrat is placed 'inside' A LIB

explanation.surface: An unscripted comment comes from a Liberal Democrat party insider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal Democrat' reads as the one British party; it splits into LIB and D, with the D put inside A LIB.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin ad libitum, at pleasure: a line made up on the spot rather than scripted.

clue.text: Feel sure about sapper’s cap

indicators.note: BET goes 'about' the sapper's unit

blocks.note: a sapper serves in the RE, the Royal Engineers

explanation.surface: Someone is certain about which cap a military engineer wears.
explanation.walkthrough: A sapper is a soldier of the Royal Engineers, RE; the surface fits, since soldiers wear berets.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the beret is a soft, round, flat cap.

clue.text: See unit converted, forming . . . . a unit!

definitions.note: en suite is an adjective; the definition is a noun, as in an en suite bathroom

indicators.note: a converted thing is remade into a different form

explanation.surface: A room is converted into a self-contained bathroom unit.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter reuses 'unit' on purpose: the dots and exclamation mark point out that the fodder's unit is rearranged into a bathroom unit.
explanation.definitionFit: British usage: an en suite is a bathroom attached to a bedroom, sold as a fitted unit.

clue.text: Miscalculate, ending in mate with bishop

indicators.note: the 'ending' of mate is its last letter

blocks.note: RR = Right Reverend, a bishop's title

explanation.surface: A chess player blunders in a mating attack with the bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is chess, but the bishop is a churchman: Right Reverend, RR.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to err is to go wrong, and a miscalculation is one way of doing it.

clue.text: Lose heart, as pride injured

indicators.note: injured letters are damaged out of their order

blocks.note: used as printed, first part of the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone gives up hope after their pride is hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' looks like a link word but is part of the fodder: AS PRIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: heart here is courage or hope, and to despair is to lose all hope.

clue.text: Posed wearing silk

blocks.note: sat = posed, as for a portrait
in = wearing, as in 'in a hat'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a model posing in silk; 'posed' is SAT, and 'wearing' is IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by material: satin is a glossy weave traditionally made from silk.

clue.text: Robin arrested, stupidly pinching book

indicators.note: done stupidly, the letters come out in a muddle
to pinch is to grab and hold, so the mixed letters hold B

explanation.surface: A man called Robin was foolishly arrested for stealing a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robin' reads as a man's name; it is the bird. 'Pinching' doubles as stealing in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A folk name: the European robin is called robin redbreast for its orange-red chest.
